subject: Effective sample size with Royle 2004 Biometrics p. 108-115 N-mixture model

messages.author: 509d884113938f54
messages.subject: Effective sample size with Royle 2004 Biometrics p. 108-115 N-mixture model
parts:
I was hoping to copy an AICc table from a software program into a manuscript and realized the table actually was displaying an AIC table.  To convert AIC to AICc the software requests the effective sample size.  My guess is that the effective sample size is the number of sites.  Effective sample size seemingly is only mentioned once in the MacKenzie et al. (2006) book.  That is in the context of occupancy modeling and it mentions that number of sites is used unless sites are not independent.  I did not find the term 'effective sample size' in the Royle 2004 paper, but might have overlooked it.

I did find an post here from 2010 in which it was suggested to just stick with AIC, albeit that may have been for a different model.

In my case, I have a fairly large number of sites, ~ 700 - 3500.  So, I doubt there is any real difference between AIC and AICc, but I wanted to ask.

Thanks for any suggestions.  

Mark

messages.author: 4a15de51da4445ae
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Effective sample size with Royle 2004 Biometrics p. 108-115 N-mixture model
parts:
hi Mark,

 I don't think it's safe to say that effective sample size is the number of sites.... I don't think there's a clear answer to this question so far as computing AICc goes.   I guess there's more information about detection covariates coming from the temporal replication and vice versa for the abundance covariates. But the likelihood is the same for both effects and so it wouldn't make sense for them to have a different effective sample size.

 I recommend not using AICc for any hierarchical model in which sample size has no clear meaning.

 Other opinions on this?

regards
andy

parts:
I totally agree, though without empirical evidence of my own.

I couldn't get a straight answer on this for known-fate nest success data on phidot a few years ago and gave up. Some advice there was to use the number of days even when the visit interval was longer, which made no sense to me.

Turek & Fletcher (2012 Comput. stat & data analysis) found that AIC weights outperformed AICc weights for model averaging in a set of regression simulations.

AICc is the default for model ranking in 'secr', but I added the 'criterion' argument so users can switch (and I do).

Murray

messages.author: 0227543d81e2924c
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Effective sample size with Royle 2004 Biometrics p. 108-115 N-mixture model
parts:
For some data types (excuse the MARK-ism), the effective sample size is relatively straightforward (to the degree, at least, that there is a consensus as to how to calculate it). For example, for known fate (simplest model), it is simply the total number of 'exposure days', since each interval is considered independent of any other interval. For nest survival, number of days known alive + 1 for the interval where nest dies. For CJS and similar data types like simple multi-state, the number of releases and re-releases. Simple chain binomials and related things. 

Where things get ugly is when you have 'interesting but annoying' flavours of parameters. As Gary noted in his response to the PhiDot discussion Murray refers to (http://www.phidot.org/forum/viewtopic.php?f=1&t=914), [note in particular the stuff in italics...]

 "...early on, the effective sample size (in MARK) was always taken as the number of Bernoulli trials. So, for the CJS model, the number of animals released and re-released is taken as the effective sample size, because these releases form Bernoulli trials. Similarly for dead recoveries and known fate data types. When this philosophy got questioned was with the models that had different types of parameters. First were the robust design models, and later the occupancy models. Clearly in the simple occupancy models, psi has a different sample size than p. psi is based on the number of patches, whereas p is based on the number of visits to patches..."

In other words, for occupancy, robust design (and probably everything based on permutations or hybrids of same), there is no consensus on what constitutes the effective sample size. As such, my general recommendation for folks is: use AIC, and as an ad hoc bit of comfort assessment, try different values for effective sample size, using the standard AIC formulation, and see if its going to make much difference. If not, then AIC is no doubt safe. If you have a smallish sample, by some criterion, then perhaps there is reason to be concerned.
